implementation_notes: EF Core supplies the classic structure declaratively: mark a property as a concurrency token with [Timestamp] (SQL Server rowversion, database-generated) or [ConcurrencyCheck]/IsConcurrencyToken() (application-managed GUID or counter), and SaveChanges emits UPDATE ... WHERE Id = @p AND Version = @p; when no row matches, EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException whose Entries and GetDatabaseValuesAsync() expose current, original and database values for a merge. Without an ORM the contract is three lines of ADO.NET: run the conditional UPDATE with the version in the WHERE clause and branch on the value returned by SqlCommand.ExecuteNonQuery(). Use the EF route whenever the mapper already owns the statements; keep the hand-written form for framework-free access or statements EF does not generate - bulk operations bypass the token entirely.
pitfalls: Bulk APIs (ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete, ExecuteSqlRaw) bypass change tracking, never check the token and never bump it; a version-guarded invariant silently disappears on those paths.
A rowversion column is a poor key: it changes on every update, so anything that treats it as identity (URLs, caches, foreign keys) breaks.
Catching DbUpdateConcurrencyException and calling SaveChanges again without refreshing OriginalValues repeats the same conflict forever.
Database-generated tokens must be re-read after insert/update; an application-managed token must be regenerated on every write or the check never fires.

variants.name: Hand-written ADO.NET conditional UPDATE with rowcount test
variants.idiom_name: SqlCommand.ExecuteNonQuery() with version in the WHERE clause
variants.implementation_notes: Framework-free data access keeps the classic structure in application code: append AND Version = @seen to the UPDATE (or DELETE) statement, bind the token read with the row, and treat ExecuteNonQuery() returning 0 as the stale signal; wrap it in the caller's transaction so the check and the write commit together. This is what a Dapper-style or generated-SQL layer must do because no mapper is maintaining the token; it also remains the only option for statements EF Core cannot express. The trade-off is that every statement must be reviewed for the predicate, whereas the EF variant centralises it.
pitfalls: Forgetting to include the version column in the SET list leaves the token unchanged, so the next writer's check compares a value that no longer means 'the version I read'.
Comparing a rowversion byte[] with == compares references; compare byte-wise or let the database do the comparison in the predicate.
